classes.name: Oral bisphosphonates
classes.description: Alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate — first-line oral therapy for osteoporosis.
classes.plainDescription: A weekly or monthly pill that slows bone loss.

classes.name: IV bisphosphonate
classes.description: Zoledronic acid (Reclast) — for patients who can't tolerate oral bisphosphonates or need stronger therapy.
classes.plainDescription: A once-a-year IV infusion that slows bone loss.

classes.name: RANKL inhibitor
classes.description: Denosumab (Prolia) — alternative to bisphosphonates, especially with renal impairment.
classes.plainDescription: A shot every six months that slows bone loss.

classes.name: Anabolic bone-building agent
classes.description: Teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab — for severe osteoporosis or bisphosphonate failure.
classes.plainDescription: An injection that builds new bone rather than just slowing loss.

classes.name: SERM
classes.description: Raloxifene — for postmenopausal women who can't use estrogen or bisphosphonates.
classes.plainDescription: A daily pill that helps bones and also lowers breast-cancer risk.

records.verificationNote: Both current Alabama Medicaid PDL documents (04/01/2026 Therapeutic-Category PDL, 4 pages, and 07/01/2026 PDL Reference Tool, 28 pages -- both fetched directly from medicaid.alabama.gov and fully keyword-searched for bisphosphonate/osteoporosis/alendronate/risedronate/ibandronate/zoledronic/reclast/denosumab/prolia/teriparatide/forteo/abaloparatide/romosozumab/evenity/raloxifene/evista) contain zero mentions of any osteoporosis agent. A follow-up WebSearch for an Alabama-Medicaid-specific PA-criteria document for these agents found only a generic third-party clinical-policy portal (al-policies.exploremyplan.com) that could not be confirmed as an Alabama-Medicaid-branded, on-topic page (JS-rendered, no verifiable Alabama Medicaid caption in the fetched HTML), so it was not used as a citation. This is treated as a known structural gap in AL Medicaid's public PDL -- osteoporosis agents are not part of the published Preferred Drug List program (likely covered without a PDL-based PA/tier restriction, consistent with the source's own 'generics...available without prior approval' default), not a research failure. The specific agent below reflects standard clinical first-line guidance, not an AL Medicaid citation.

records.verificationNote: Searched the full extracted text of the cited PDF (all 193 pages) for 'zoledronic', 'reclast', and 'zometa' and found zero matches - the drug is genuinely absent from this pharmacy drug list, not a search failure. This is expected and verified as a structural gap: IV zoledronic acid for osteoporosis is typically administered in-office/infusion-center and billed under the medical benefit rather than dispensed through retail/mail pharmacy, so it would not appear on a pharmacy PDL like this one regardless of coverage status. The preferred-agent identity, strength, and sig above are standard drug-reference facts (not read from this document, since the document doesn't cover it) - a member would need to check Blue Cross AL's medical-benefit policy/PA criteria separately, not this PDL.

records.preferredRestriction: Not found in the Part D drug list at all — zoledronic acid/Reclast for osteoporosis is typically billed under Medicare Part B (medical benefit, physician-administered infusion) rather than through the Part D pharmacy formulary; confirm actual Part B coverage/PA requirements directly with Blue Advantage Member Services rather than this document.
records.verificationNote: Full-text searched all 116 pages of the Blue Advantage Choice 2026 formulary (H0104_CHF26_C, updated 01/20/2026) for 'zoledronic' and 'Reclast', and read the complete 'Metabolic Bone Disease Agents' section verbatim (pdf pages 80-81, printed pages 66-67) — no zoledronic acid/Reclast entry exists anywhere in the document. This is consistent with standard Medicare benefit design: IV zoledronic acid administered in a physician's office for osteoporosis is typically billed under Part B (medical benefit) rather than Part D (pharmacy formulary), so its absence from this Part D drug list does not necessarily mean the plan won't cover it — it means coverage falls outside this document's scope entirely. The preferredAgent/sig fields reflect the standard real-world zoledronic acid regimen (inferred, not read from this source) rather than a formulary-stated value, hence 'partial' verification.
